rubric.name: Stove burner left on, knobs freely usable
rubric.modifier: Forgetting a lit burner and misjudging heat are core dementia fire/burn risks; a person may turn knobs on repeatedly. Fix: knob covers, automatic shut-off device, or disconnect the stove.

citation.line: Use stove knob covers or remove knobs, shut off gas when not cooking, prefer appliances with automatic shut-off.

rubric.name: Knives and sharps out on the counter
rubric.modifier: Judgment about sharp objects declines; knives should be locked away rather than left in the open.

citation.line: Lock up or remove knives, scissors and other sharp items.

rubric.name: Cleaning chemicals out and unlocked
rubric.modifier: Colorful pods and bottles can be mistaken for food or drink by a person with dementia (ingestion/poisoning).

citation.line: Keep bleach and laundry pods out of sight, secured, in original containers so they are not swallowed.

rubric.name: Medication bottles left out
rubric.modifier: Unsupervised access risks double-dosing or skipped doses; medications should be locked and dispensed by a caregiver.

citation.line: Clear prescription drugs and vitamins off counters and tables; lock medications away.

rubric.name: Razor and medications out on the sink
rubric.modifier: Sharps and medications in the bathroom are a common unsupervised-access point.

citation.line: Lock away medicines and sharp items (razors) in the bathroom.

rubric.name: White toilet seat on white toilet and floor (low contrast)
rubric.modifier: Reduced contrast sensitivity makes a white-on-white toilet hard to locate; a colored seat helps with toileting and sitting safely.

citation.line: Choose a toilet seat and fittings that contrast with wall and floor so they can be found.

rubric.name: Dark bath mat on a light floor
rubric.modifier: A dark mat can be perceived as a hole or step by someone with dementia, causing freezing, stepping over, or falls.

citation.line: Dark rugs and mats can look like obstacles or holes in the floor.

rubric.name: Plugged-in hair dryer by the sink
rubric.modifier: Electrical appliances near water are a shock risk when judgment is impaired.

citation.line: Remove small electrical appliances from the bathroom and cover outlets.

rubric.name: Large mirror facing the bed
rubric.modifier: A person with dementia may not recognize their own reflection and think a stranger is in the room, causing fear or agitation.

citation.line: Use fewer, smaller, carefully placed mirrors; reflections can confuse (Alzheimer's Society: remove or cover them).

rubric.name: Bold high-contrast patterned rug
rubric.modifier: Busy patterns can be misread as steps, objects or holes, causing hesitation, reaching for things that are not there, or falls.

citation.line: Avoid busy patterns; a change in floor pattern can be mistaken for a step because depth perception changes.

rubric.name: Space heater next to bedding
rubric.modifier: Portable heaters near fabric are a fire and burn risk that a person with dementia may not recognize.

citation.line: Remove portable space heaters.

rubric.name: Car keys hanging by the front door
rubric.modifier: Visible car keys invite unsafe driving once driving has stopped; keys should be kept out of sight.

citation.line: Remove access to car keys once the person no longer drives.

rubric.name: Front door left open to the outside
rubric.modifier: Six in ten people with dementia will wander; an unsecured, open exit is the main wandering pathway.

citation.line: Most people with dementia will wander; secure exterior doors (deadbolts out of eye line), disguise exits or add door alerts.

rubric.name: Clutter piles in the walkway
rubric.modifier: Clutter increases falls and confusion; visual crowding makes navigation harder for people with dementia.

citation.line: Remove throw rugs, cords and extra clutter; keep floors clear.

levels.name: Obvious
levels.description: One salient hazard, clean room, good light, original base rooms.

levels.name: Subtle
levels.description: One hazard that requires judging ADEQUACY (towel bar used as grab bar, short handrail, low-contrast mat) or is small / partially occluded.

levels.name: Compound
levels.description: Two hazards stacked in one room plus one SAFE look-alike distractor (e.g. a proper anchored grab bar, a flat non-slip mat) that must NOT be flagged.

levels.name: Cluttered
levels.description: 3-4 hazards (some subtle) plus 2 distractors, with realism degradations: dim or night lighting, soft focus/noise, new base homes.

levels.name: Adversarial
levels.description: ~40% safe-but-scary rooms (0 hazards, only look-alikes: negatives) and ~60% rooms with 4+ hazards, several subtle adequacy/measurement ones, in poor light.

method: Label-before-pixels: Sonnet 5 (Bedrock) plans each edit's label+region, Stability inpaint (Bedrock) paints one region per step on a clean base; box = pixel diff between consecutive steps. Distractors are labelled negatives. Conditions are deterministic global grades applied last. New bases: Stability control-structure restyles of existing clean rooms (no Stability text-to-image model is enabled on this account), judge-checked for hazards.

cost.note: final generation run counters + ~$3/bench for earlier Bedrock runs, refine/re-judge and the 8-model curve (~160 VLM calls/bench); estimates, not invoices
